In the middle only the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is nonzero, which pulls an equal square across the fibres. From the lengthening \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,a\) we get \(E_{\mathrm{y}}\), and from the contraction \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,a\) we get \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\). This square too stays a rectangle.

For an isotropic material all three moduli equal Young's modulus \(E\) (definition 3.1), all Poisson's ratios equal \(\nu\) (definition 3.8) and all shear moduli equal \(G\) (definition 3.17). For an orthotropic one, however, \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\) can be different numbers, so the order of the indices matters. Why are they different with fibres? When we pull across the fibres, the square has to contract along them, and the stiff fibres resist contraction as much as stretching. The contraction is therefore small compared with the large lengthening, and \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\) is small. For the composite of section 3.4.7 we will have \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}26\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0{,}01268\). CM and SADD label the material axes \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) instead of \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and SADD writes the shear moduli with \(\mu\).

From the engineering constants we build the material compliance matrix in steps.

  1. By steps 1 to 5 and 7 of the proof of corollary 3.33 on the stiffness matrix of an orthotropic material, which do not use the symmetry of \(\mat C\), \(\mat C^{-1}\) has zeros at the same places as \(\mat C\). Normal stresses therefore cause no shear in the material axes, and the shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) causes only the shear \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), likewise for the other two.
  2. The product of a matrix and a column is, by definition 1.97, the sum of the columns of the matrix multiplied by the elements of the column, since the element of the product at place \(p\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{q}} (\mat C^{-1})_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{q}}\). If only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is nonzero, \(\{\varepsilon\}\) is therefore the first column of the matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\) multiplied by \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  3. By definition 3.34 in this case \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by step 1 there is no shear, the square stays a rectangle. The first column of the matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\) therefore has the elements \(1/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(0\), \(0\) and \(0\).
  4. Likewise we get the second column from a stress in the direction \(y\) alone and the third from a stress in the direction \(z\) alone.
  5. If only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is nonzero, then \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}/G_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and all other strains are zero by step 1. The fourth column therefore has the number \(1/G_{\mathrm{yz}}\) at place \(4\) and zero elsewhere. Likewise we get the fifth column with \(G_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and the sixth with \(G_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  6. All six columns together give the relation \(\{\varepsilon\} = \mat C^{-1}\{\sigma\}\) with the columns of definition 3.27 and the compliance matrix \(\mat C^{-1}\), which is
    \[\begin{bmatrix} 1/E_{\mathrm{x}} & -\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}} & -\nu_{\mathrm{zx}}/E_{\mathrm{z}} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}} & 1/E_{\mathrm{y}} & -\nu_{\mathrm{zy}}/E_{\mathrm{z}} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}/E_{\mathrm{x}} & -\nu_{\mathrm{yz}}/E_{\mathrm{y}} & 1/E_{\mathrm{z}} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/G_{\mathrm{yz}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/G_{\mathrm{xz}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/G_{\mathrm{xy}} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{3.42}\]

Let us look at the block as a picture too: \(\mat C^{-1}\) with its labels \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) along the edges, on a grid of cells. The block of three times three cells is the only part of the matrix with nonzero elements off the diagonal, elsewhere there are only reciprocal shear moduli on the diagonal. On the main diagonal stand \(1/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(1/E_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(1/E_{\mathrm{z}}\). The element in row 1 and column 2 is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the element in row 2 and column 1 is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\). Likewise face each other across the diagonal the elements 13 and 31 and the elements 23 and 32. The dashed diagonal is a mirror axis: the matrix is symmetric if the two elements of each pair are equal.

By step 2 this equation says that the strains of the six simple tests add up when all stresses act at once (CM (6.3.20)-(6.3.23), PDF pp. 263-264). The matrix does not look symmetric: in row 1 and column 2 stands \(-\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}}\), in row 2 and column 1 \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\). And yet it must be.

Corollary 3.35 Reciprocal relations (recipročne zveze)

Let a material at the point \(P\) be orthotropic, with planes of material symmetry perpendicular to the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and let its material stiffness matrix be symmetric and have an inverse matrix. Then

\[\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} = \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} , \qquad \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} = \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{zx}}}{E_{\mathrm{z}}} , \qquad \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{yz}}}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} = \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{zy}}}{E_{\mathrm{z}}} . \tag{3.43}\]
Proof

We have to show that the material compliance matrix is symmetric, and compare its elements.

  1. By the definition of the inverse matrix 1.110, \(\mat C\,\mat C^{-1} = \mat I\) and \(\mat C^{-1}\,\mat C = \mat I\).
  2. We transpose the first equality. By lemma 1.102, \((\mat C\,\mat C^{-1})^\T = (\mat C^{-1})^\T\,\mat C^\T\), and \(\mat I^\T = \mat I\). Since \(\mat C^\T = \mat C\), we get \((\mat C^{-1})^\T\,\mat C = \mat I\).
  3. Likewise from the second equality we get \(\mat C\,(\mat C^{-1})^\T = \mat I\).
  4. By steps 2 and 3, \((\mat C^{-1})^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat C\). There is only one inverse matrix (lemma 1.111 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix), so \((\mat C^{-1})^\T = \mat C^{-1}\), and the material compliance matrix is symmetric.
  5. In (3.42) the element in row 1 and column 2 is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the element in row 2 and column 1 is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\). By step 4 they are equal, which is the first equality of (3.43).
  6. The elements in row 1 and column 3 and in row 3 and column 1 give the second equality, and the elements in row 2 and column 3 and in row 3 and column 2 the third.

Source: CM (6.3.24) (PDF p. 265), SADD, PDF p. 336, BOWER, PDF p. 110.

There are twelve engineering constants, and the reciprocal relations express three of them by the others. Nine remain, as many as the constants in (3.41): \(E_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\nu_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (CM (6.3.25), PDF p. 265). The reciprocal relations hold only if the material stiffness matrix is symmetric, which we will prove for an ideally elastic material with theorem 3.62 in section 3.6. Without this symmetry all twelve engineering constants would be independent.

What do the reciprocal relations mean? Let us pull an equal square once along the fibres and once across them with the same stress \(\sigma\). The lateral strain is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma/E_{\mathrm{x}}\) the first time and \(-\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\sigma/E_{\mathrm{y}}\) the second, and the first reciprocal relation says that they are equal: the contraction on the left equals the contraction in the middle, although the lengthenings are very different. Tension in the direction \(x\) contracts the direction \(y\) exactly as much as an equal tension in the direction \(y\) contracts the direction \(x\). Without the symmetry the two contractions in the figure could differ. We will check this with numbers on the strip of composite.

3.4.5 Transversely isotropic and isotropic material

Some materials are the same in all directions perpendicular to some axis. Such are crystals with a hexagonal structure, for example zinc, magnesium and titanium, in the plane perpendicular to the sixfold axis of the crystal (BOWER §3.2.15, PDF p. 112). Figure 3.132 shows the atoms in this plane. Neighbours are \(a\) apart along the axis \(x\). After a turn by a sixth of a revolution, \(60^\circ\), the new axis \(\bar x\) again points along a row of atoms with spacing \(a\), and the lattice looks the same. After a turn by \(30^\circ\), however, it points between the rows, where neighbouring atoms are \(a\sqrt3\) apart, and the lattice looks different. Even so, the turn by a sixth of a revolution alone forces the elastic constants into the form that is the same after every turn about this axis (checked with SymPy). The constants are therefore the same in all directions of the plane, although the lattice is not.

For a composite with parallel fibres let us assume that the fibres are distributed over the cross section without a preferred direction. Then, by Neumann's principle from the beginning of section 3.4.3, it is the same in all directions perpendicular to the fibres. We describe the directions perpendicular to the axis by a turn of the old axes into the new ones about it, with pairs of numbers \(c\) and \(s\) for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), as in section 2.9.

Definition 3.36 Transversely isotropic material (prečno izotropen material)

A material is transversely isotropic (prečno izotropen) at the point \(P\) about the axis \(z\) if it has the same elastic constants in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with origin at \(P\) that are obtained from the chosen one by turning the axes \(x\) and \(y\) about the axis \(z\). These are the systems with the unit vectors of the axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-s, c, 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\) for any numbers \(c\) and \(s\) with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). The plane through \(P\) perpendicular to the axis \(z\) is called the plane of isotropy (ravnina izotropije).

Source: SADD §11.2.3 (PDF pp. 336-337), BOWER §3.2.14 (PDF pp. 110-111).

The vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) are unit vectors, because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), and perpendicular, because their scalar product is \(-cs + sc = 0\). BOWER treats a transversely isotropic material as a special orthotropic material (BOWER, PDF p. 110), so in the lemma we assume the form (3.41). This is an assumption, so let us say why we may make it and what it changes. We may make it because the demand for the same constants under all turns about the axis \(z\) already contains it: SADD derives the five constants from these turns alone (SADD (11.2.11)-(11.2.12), PDF pp. 336-337), and we checked with SymPy that of the 21 constants of a symmetric matrix the turns with \(c = 0\), \(s = 1\), with \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\) and with \(c = 12/13\), \(s = 5/13\) leave the same five, while all the elements that (3.41) does not have are zero. The assumption therefore does not change the result, but it shortens the proof, because only four equalities among nine constants are left to show. The lemma itself is proved only for matrices of this form.

For two turns we will require that the material has the same constants in the new axes. Let us draw both.

The first is the turn by a quarter revolution about the axis \(z\) (figure 3.133). Next to the old axes \(x\) and \(y\) we draw the new ones: the axis \(\bar x\) points where the old axis \(y\) does, and the axis \(\bar y\) points against the old axis \(x\). We look at a small square of material along the axis \(z\). On its top face, whose normal points in the direction \(y\), acts the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). In the new axes the same face has its normal in the direction \(\bar x\), so the same arrow is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) there. The right face has its normal in the direction \(x\), against \(\bar y\), and the normal stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on it is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) in the new axes. The shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) on the top face points in the direction \(x\), that is against \(\bar y\), so \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). The shear stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) on the right face equals it by theorem 2.41 on the symmetry of stress. On the right the same is written for all nine components. The left table holds the components of an arbitrary matrix \(\mat A\) in the old axes, the right table the components in the new axes, written with the old ones. The turn swaps the diagonal elements \(xx\) and \(yy\). It swaps the elements \(xy\) and \(yx\) and reverses their signs. It swaps the elements of the column \(z\) and reverses the sign of one, likewise the elements of the row \(z\), and it leaves the element \(zz\) alone.

The second turn puts the new axes onto the diagonals (figure 3.134). A square with sides along the axes \(x\) and \(y\) has its diagonals in the directions of the new unit vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\), which are drawn to the side. The shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = g\) changes it into a rhombus. The centre stays in place and the diagonals of the rhombus point in the same directions as before. A half diagonal of length \(h\) lengthens by \(g\,h\) in the direction \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and shortens by \(g\,h\) in the direction \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\). A shear in the old axes is therefore, in the new axes, a strain \(g\) along one diagonal and a strain \(-g\) along the other.

Lemma 3.37 Constants of a transversely isotropic material (konstante prečno izotropnega materiala)

Let a material at the point \(P\) obey the generalized Hooke's law with a symmetric material stiffness matrix of the form (3.41) and let it be transversely isotropic about the axis \(z\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} C_{22} &= C_{11} , & C_{23} &= C_{13} , \\ C_{55} &= C_{44} , & C_{66} &= \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12}) , \end{aligned} \tag{3.44}\]

and the material has five constants, \(C_{11}\), \(C_{12}\), \(C_{13}\), \(C_{33}\) and \(C_{44}\).

Proof

We have to show four equalities. The first three follow from the turn by a quarter revolution, the fourth from the turn onto the diagonals. In both cases we compute the components in the new axes by the rules (2.59) and lemma 2.55, written in components, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\)\(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}} = Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ab}} = Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\), where the rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are the unit vectors of the new axes written in the old axes.

1. The turn by a quarter revolution.

  1. For \(c = 0\) and \(s = 1\) we have \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (0, 1, 0) = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 0, 0) = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) (the new axes in figure 3.133). The nonzero elements of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yx}} = -1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1\).
  2. Each row of \(\mat Q\) has a single nonzero element, so each double sum has a single term. We get \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = Q_{\mathrm{yx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,Q_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). In figure 3.133 these are the diagonal elements, the element \(zz\), the elements of the column \(z\) and the element \(xy\) of the right table, and on the square the arrows \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\). The same holds for the strains, so also \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\).
  3. The material has the same constants in the new axes. The first row of (3.41) in the new axes is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{12}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{13}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and with step 2, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{12}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  4. The second row of (3.41) in the old axes is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{12}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{22}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{23}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  5. We subtract the equations of steps 3 and 4 and get \(0 = (C_{11} - C_{22})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + (C_{13} - C_{23})\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) for every small strain. With the strain in which only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}001\) is nonzero we get \(C_{22} = C_{11}\), with the strain in which only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0{,}001\) is nonzero, \(C_{23} = C_{13}\).
  6. The fourth row in the new axes is \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = C_{44}\,\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and with step 2, \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -C_{44}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The fifth row in the old axes is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = C_{55}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\). With the strain in which only \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\) is nonzero we get \(C_{55} = C_{44}\).

2. The turn onto the diagonals.

  1. For \(c = s = 1/\sqrt2\), which gives \(c^2 + s^2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1\), we have \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\). The new axes \(x\) and \(y\) point along the diagonals of a square with sides along the old axes (figure 3.134, the vectors \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\)). The nonzero elements of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = Q_{\mathrm{yy}} = 1/\sqrt2\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yx}} = -1/\sqrt2\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1\).
  2. Take the strain with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = g\), where \(g = 0{,}0005\), so \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}001\), and all other components zero. Such a shear in the plane \(xy\) is given, for example, by the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = g\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = g\,x\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), which changes the square into a rhombus.
  3. In the old axes, by the sixth row of (3.41), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\,C_{66}\,g\). The other stresses are zero, because the other elements of the sixth column are zero.
  4. In the sum for \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ab}}\) only the terms with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\) remain, so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ab}} = (Q_{\mathrm{ax}}\,Q_{\mathrm{by}} + Q_{\mathrm{ay}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bx}})\,g\). Thus \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,g = g\) (the lengthening of a half diagonal), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 2 \cdot \big({-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}}\big) \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,g = -g\) (the shortening of the other) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \big(\tfrac12 - \tfrac12\big)\,g = 0\) (the diagonals of the rhombus stay perpendicular). The components with an index \(z\) are zero, because \(Q_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zy}}\) are zero.
  5. The material has the same constants in the new axes. The first row of (3.41) in the new axes gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,g + C_{12}\,(-g) = (C_{11} - C_{12})\,g\).
  6. We compute the same stress also from the stresses in the old axes. Only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\) are nonzero, so \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2\,Q_{\mathrm{xx}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 2\,C_{66}\,g = 2\,C_{66}\,g\).
  7. Steps 5 and 6 give \((C_{11} - C_{12})\,g = 2\,C_{66}\,g\). Since \(g \ne 0\), \(C_{66} = \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12})\).

3. Counting.

  1. Of the nine constants in (3.41), the four equalities (3.44) express \(C_{22}\), \(C_{23}\), \(C_{55}\) and \(C_{66}\) by the others. Five constants remain.

Source: SADD (11.2.12) (PDF pp. 336-337), BOWER §3.2.14 (PDF pp. 110-111). The proof with two turns is not from the sources. The converse, that a material with these five constants stays the same under every turn about the axis \(z\), is not proved in the two sources, and we prove it in the next lemma.

Why is the shear constant in the plane of isotropy not a new constant? Step 4 of the second part shows that a shear in the plane \(xy\) is the same as a stretch in the direction of one diagonal and an equally large contraction in the direction of the other (figure 3.134). The diagonals point in the directions of the new axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\). A material that is the same in all directions of the plane responds to a stretch of the diagonal in the same way as to a stretch along the axis \(x\), with the constants \(C_{11}\) and \(C_{12}\). That is why the stiffness in shear is determined by them. For an isotropic material we met the same in section 3.2, when we expressed the shear modulus by Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio.

Lemma 3.37 showed what transverse isotropy demands: the four equalities (3.44). Does the converse hold? Definition 3.36 demands the same constants under every turn about the axis \(z\), for any numbers \(c\) and \(s\) with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), and we looked at only two turns: the quarter turn and the turn onto the diagonals. A material could be the same under these two turns but not under others. BOWER says that the response of a material with a plane of isotropy does not change when it is turned about one axis (BOWER, PDF pp. 110 and 112). SADD calls a material that is the same under every turn about the axis \(z\) transversely isotropic and derives the five constants from this (SADD (11.2.11)-(11.2.12), PDF pp. 336-337). Neither of them writes down a proof of the converse. Let us give one.

Let us draw what the lemma claims (figure 3.135). On the left is the plane of isotropy, in which the fibre ends are spread without a preferred direction. In it are drawn the old axes \(x\) and \(y\) with the unit vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the turned axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) with the unit vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\). In the middle are the old axes, the square of side \(a\) before the strain and the square after the stretch in the direction \(x\), which lengthens the side by \(0{,}001\,a\). On the right are the old axes again, and next to them the square along the new axes before the strain (the square) and after the same strain (the parallelogram). The blackwhite arrows are the stresses that we will compute in the example after the lemma: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) on the faces of the old square, and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and the shear stress \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) on the faces of the turned one.

The idea shows when we write the law with five constants a little differently. By the fourth equality (3.44), \(C_{11} = C_{12} + 2C_{66}\), so the first row of (3.41) reads

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{12}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = C_{12}\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} .\]

The second row is the same, except that \(2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) stands at the end, and the sixth is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). In the plane \(xy\) the law therefore has the form of Hooke's law of an isotropic material (3.28). Every stress component in the plane is \(2C_{66}\) times the same strain component, and the normal ones get in addition a common part that depends only on the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and on \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The role of the number \(2\mu\) is played here by \(2C_{66}\). A turn about the axis \(z\) does not change the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) or the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and the components in the plane change by the same rule as the stresses. That is why the law keeps its form. Why the sum does not change is shown in figure 3.135. The sum is the fraction by which the area of a piece in the plane grows, just as the trace is the fraction by which the volume grows (section 1.17.4). The square along the old axes becomes a rectangle and the square along the new axes a parallelogram. The area of both grows by the same fraction, because the strain is the same and we only cut the square out differently.

Lemma 3.38 Five constants suffice for transverse isotropy (pet konstant zadošča za prečno izotropnost)

Let a material at the point \(P\) obey the generalized Hooke's law with a symmetric material stiffness matrix of the form (3.41) whose elements satisfy the equalities (3.44), and let \(c\) and \(s\) be numbers with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). Then the material has the same elastic constants also in the rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with origin at \(P\) and with the unit vectors of the axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-s, c, 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = (0, 0, 1)\). The material is therefore transversely isotropic about the axis \(z\).

Proof

We have to show that the stress and strain components in the new axes satisfy, for every small strain, the same equations as in the old ones. A bar marks the components in the new axes.

  1. The law in the old axes. By the equalities (3.44), \(C_{22} = C_{11}\), \(C_{23} = C_{13}\), \(C_{55} = C_{44}\) and \(C_{11} = C_{12} + 2C_{66}\). Equation (3.39) with the matrix (3.41) and with the engineering shear strains \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (definition 3.27) therefore reads, row by row,
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} &= C_{13}\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{33}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} &= 2C_{44}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} , & \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} &= 2C_{44}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} , \end{aligned} \tag{3.45}\]
    where \(p = C_{12}\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). In \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) we wrote \(C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) as \(C_{12}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) likewise \(C_{22}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The letter \(p\) is not a pressure here.
  2. The rules for the new components. The rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) has the rows \((c, s, 0)\), \((-s, c, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\) (definition 2.44), the unit vectors of the new axes in figure 3.135. By theorem 2.53 on the transformation of stress components the new stress components are therefore given by the equations (2.60). By lemma 2.55 the strains change by the same rule, \(\bar{\ten\varepsilon} = \mat Q\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Q^\T\), and they are symmetric (definition 1.121), so the equations (2.60) hold for them with the letter \(\varepsilon\) instead of \(\sigma\).
  3. What does not change. The last equation (2.60) for the strains gives \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). We add the first two:
    \[\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = (c^2 + s^2)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + (s^2 + c^2)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + (2cs - 2cs)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} ,\]
    because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). The number \(\bar p = C_{12}\,(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{13}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is therefore equal to \(p\). In figure 3.135 this is the equal fraction by which the areas of the old and of the turned square grow.
  4. The normal stress \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). We insert the law of step 1 into the first equation (2.60):
    \[\begin{aligned} \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= c^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + s^2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2cs\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ &= c^2\,(p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}) + s^2\,(p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + 2cs \cdot 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} . \end{aligned}\]
  5. We collect the terms with \(p\) and the terms with \(2C_{66}\): \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (c^2 + s^2)\,p + 2C_{66}\,(c^2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + s^2\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + 2cs\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}})\).
  6. The first bracket is \(1\), and by step 3, \(p = \bar p\). The second bracket is \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by the first equation (2.60) for the strains. Therefore \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \bar p + 2C_{66}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). In the same way the second equation gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \bar p + 2C_{66}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\).
  7. Shear in the plane. We insert the law of step 1 into the third equation (2.60):
    \[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -cs\,(p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}) + cs\,(p + 2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + (c^2 - s^2)\,2C_{66}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
    The two terms with \(p\) cancel. What remains is \(2C_{66}\,\big({-cs}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\big)\), which by the third equation for the strains is \(2C_{66}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  8. Shear with an index \(z\). We insert the law of step 1 into the fourth row of (2.60) and take out \(2C_{44}\): \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2C_{44}\,(c\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} + s\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}})\). By the same row for the strains the bracket is \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), so \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2C_{44}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). Likewise \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + c\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2C_{44}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\).
  9. The normal stress \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The last equation (2.60) gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). By step 1 this is \(C_{13}\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{33}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and by step 3 it is \(C_{13}\,(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}) + C_{33}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  10. Steps 6 to 9 are the equations (3.45) with a bar on all components. Read backwards as in step 1, they are the rows of the equation \(\{\bar\sigma\} = \mat C\,\{\bar\varepsilon\}\) with the same matrix \(\mat C\).
  11. By steps 1 to 4 of the proof of lemma 3.28, each row of (3.39) is the equation (3.37) for the pair of indices of its place, with the two equal shear terms collected, and the equation for the pair in the reverse order has the same constants. The matrix \(\bar{\ten\sigma}\) is symmetric (section 2.9, after theorem 2.53). The numbers \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) therefore satisfy the generalized Hooke's law (3.37) for every small strain also in the new system, and by definition 3.25 they are the elastic constants of the material in the new system.
  12. The numbers \(c\) and \(s\) were any numbers with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). The material therefore has the same constants in all systems of definition 3.36 and is transversely isotropic about the axis \(z\).

Source: BOWER §3.2.14-3.2.15 (PDF pp. 110-112), SADD §11.2.3, (11.2.11)-(11.2.12) (PDF pp. 336-337). The proof is not from the sources. We checked the algebra of steps 3 to 9 with SymPy.

The proof confirmed the idea from before the lemma and completed it in step 8: the shear components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) turn like the components of a vector in the plane, and the shear stresses with them. We used the condition \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) in steps 3 and 6, where it made sure that the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) does not change and that the number in front of \(p\) is \(1\). Together with lemma 3.37 the lemma says that a material with a symmetric material stiffness matrix of the form (3.41) is transversely isotropic about the axis \(z\) exactly when the four equalities (3.44) hold.

The bound \(0{,}001\) for a small strain holds for the components in the system in which we write the law, and a turn can double it. We express the old components by the new ones, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c^2\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + s^2\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - 2cs\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), and since all three new components can be \(\pm 0{,}001\) with signs that add every term, the largest value is \((c^2 + s^2 + 2|cs|) \cdot 0{,}001 = (1 + 2|cs|) \cdot 0{,}001\). Because \(2|cs| \le c^2 + s^2 = 1\), this is at most \(0{,}002\), reached at \(|c| = |s| = 1/\sqrt2\) (over all elements of the matrix SymPy gave the largest factor \(2\), smaller for elements with an index \(z\), for example at \(c = s = 1/\sqrt2\) \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}001\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}001\) give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}002\)). This does not change the conclusion, because the equalities of the lemmas follow from the rules of the turn, not from the size of the strain, and the law is linear: the bound only decides for which strains we use it, and in the other system it is twice as large. The same holds in corollary 3.39, where turns about the axes \(z\) and \(x\) and reversed axes appear, with a factor of at most \(2\).

Let us test the lemma with numbers on a crystal of titanium, which has a hexagonal lattice. Let the axis \(z\) be perpendicular to the basal plane of the lattice. By BOWER (table 3.3, PDF p. 112) its constants are \(C_{11} = 162{,}4\) GPa, \(C_{12} = 92\) GPa, \(C_{13} = 69\) GPa, \(C_{33} = 180{,}7\) GPa and \(C_{44} = 46{,}7\) GPa, and by the fourth equality (3.44), \(C_{66} = \tfrac12\,(162{,}4 - 92)\) GPa \(= 35{,}2\) GPa. Take the strain whose only nonzero component is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\), and the axes turned with \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\) (figure 3.135). We compute the stresses in the new axes in two ways, all with SymPy.

  1. In the old axes. By (3.45), \(p = 92\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 92\) MPa, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 92\ \text{MPa} + 70{,}4\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 162{,}4\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 92\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 69\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 69\) MPa. There are no shear stresses.
  2. With the rule for the new components (2.60): \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}36 \cdot 162{,}4 + 0{,}64 \cdot 92 = 117{,}344\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}64 \cdot 162{,}4 + 0{,}36 \cdot 92 = 137{,}056\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}48 \cdot 162{,}4 + 0{,}48 \cdot 92 = -33{,}792\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 69\) MPa.
  3. With the law in the new axes. By the same rule for the strains, \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}36 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}00036\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}64 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}00064\) and \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}48 \cdot 0{,}001 = -0{,}00048\), so \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -0{,}00096\), and the other components are zero. Then \(\bar p = 92\ \text{GPa} \cdot (0{,}00036 + 0{,}00064) = 92\) MPa, and (3.45) with the same constants gives \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 92\ \text{MPa} + 70{,}4\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}00036 = 117{,}344\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 92\ \text{MPa} + 70{,}4\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}00064 = 137{,}056\) MPa, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 35{,}2\ \text{GPa} \cdot (-0{,}00096) = -33{,}792\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 69\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 = 69\) MPa.

Both ways give the same stresses. In the new axes the same strain also has a shear: a square along the new axes becomes a parallelogram (figure 3.135, right). The law gives the shear stress that goes with it, which is negative because it points against the axis \(\bar y\), exactly through the constant \(C_{66}\) that the fourth equality fixed. If the material had all other constants the same and \(C_{66}\) equal to, for example, \(C_{44} = 46{,}7\) GPa, the law in the new axes would give \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 46{,}7\ \text{GPa} \cdot (-0{,}00096) = -44{,}832\) MPa. The rule for the new components would still give \(-33{,}792\) MPa, because for this strain the stresses in the old axes do not depend on \(C_{66}\). Such a material would not have the same constants in the turned axes.

An isotropic material is the same in all directions, so it is transversely isotropic about every axis. CM describes it as a material with infinitely many planes of symmetry (CM, PDF p. 266). The path from 21 constants ends with it. Figure 3.136 shows all the patterns of this path side by side.

From left to right are the triclinic material, the monoclinic material, the orthotropic material, the transversely isotropic material and the isotropic material, and under each table is the number of independent constants.

Corollary 3.39 Stiffness matrix of an isotropic material (togostna matrika izotropnega materiala)

Let a material at the point \(P\) obey the generalized Hooke's law with a symmetric material stiffness matrix \(\mat C\) and let it have the same elastic constants in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with origin at \(P\). Then

\[C_{11} = C_{22} = C_{33} , \qquad C_{12} = C_{13} = C_{23} , \qquad C_{44} = C_{55} = C_{66} = \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12}) ,\]

all other elements above the diagonal are zero, and with \(\lambda = C_{12}\) and \(\mu = C_{44}\) the matrix \(\mat C\) is the matrix (3.40).

Proof

We have to show that the listed equalities follow from equal constants in all systems, and compare them with (3.40), the last pattern of figure 3.136.

  1. The material has the same constants also in the systems with a reversed axis \(x\), \(y\) or \(z\). By definition 3.29 the planes through \(P\) perpendicular to the axes are therefore planes of material symmetry, and by corollary 3.33 on the stiffness matrix of an orthotropic material \(\mat C\) has the form (3.41), the third pattern in figure 3.136.
  2. It has the same constants in all systems turned about the axis \(z\), so it is transversely isotropic about the axis \(z\). By lemma 3.37 on the constants of a transversely isotropic material, \(C_{22} = C_{11}\), \(C_{23} = C_{13}\), \(C_{55} = C_{44}\) and \(C_{66} = \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12})\), the fourth pattern.
  3. It is also transversely isotropic about the axis \(x\). In the lemma the axis \(z\) plays no special role. When the axis \(x\) takes over the role of the axis \(z\), and the axes \(y\) and \(z\) the roles of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the places \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), \(5\) and \(6\) are mapped to the places \(2\), \(3\), \(1\), \(5\), \(6\) and \(4\). Place \(4\), for example, is the pair \(\bar y\bar z\) of the new axes, which is the pair \(zx\) of the old ones, so place \(5\). The lemma then gives \(C_{33} = C_{22}\), \(C_{13} = C_{12}\), \(C_{66} = C_{55}\) and \(C_{44} = \tfrac12\,(C_{22} - C_{23})\).
  4. From steps 2 and 3 it follows for the last pattern that \(C_{11} = C_{22} = C_{33}\), \(C_{12} = C_{13} = C_{23}\) and \(C_{44} = C_{55} = C_{66}\), and by step 2 this number equals \(\tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12})\).
  5. With \(\lambda = C_{12}\) and \(\mu = C_{44}\) we have \(C_{11} = C_{12} + 2\,C_{44} = \lambda + 2\mu\). The matrix therefore equals (3.40), the last pattern with two independent constants.

Source: CM (6.3.38)-(6.3.39) (PDF p. 267), SADD (11.2.16) (PDF p. 338).

The path from 21 constants has led us exactly to the matrix that in section 3.4.2 we copied from Hooke's law (3.28). The Lamé constants are thus the element \(C_{12}\), which tells how much lateral stress a stretch causes, and the element \(C_{44}\), which tells how much shear stress a shear causes.

Between the orthotropic material with nine constants and the isotropic one with two, the funnel in figure 3.114 has three intermediate stages. The stage with five, the transversely isotropic material, has been derived. The stages with six and with three constants remain. They need no new calculation, because the first part of the proof of lemma 3.37 uses a single turn, the quarter turn about the axis \(z\).

Which material is the same after a quarter turn but not after other turns? Let us look at the structure of a crystal in which the atoms lie at the corners of boxes with a square base.

On the left of figure 3.138 we look along the axis \(z\). The atoms lie on a square net, neighbours are \(a\) apart in the direction \(x\) and the same in the direction \(y\) (axes). After the quarter turn the new axis \(\bar x\) points where the old axis \(y\) did, so again along a row of atoms with spacing \(a\). In the new axes the lattice looks exactly as it does in the old ones. The axes turned by \(45^\circ\), however, point along the diagonals of the squares, where neighbouring atoms are \(a\sqrt2\) apart, and there the lattice looks different. On the right we look along the axis \(y\). In the direction \(z\) the atoms are \(c\) apart, and \(c\) differs from \(a\). A quarter turn about the axis \(y\) would put the axis \(x\) onto the axis \(z\), rows with spacing \(a\) onto rows with spacing \(c\), so the lattice is not the same after it. The crystal is the same after a quarter turn about one axis only.

Why does the same structure mean the same constants? The elastic constants are a property of the structure. If the structure looks exactly the same in the new axes as in the old ones, no test tells one set of axes from the other, so the same strain, written in either set of axes, goes with the same stresses. We reasoned this way already for the mirror image in section 3.4.3.

Such a material is called tetragonal. The name comes from the Greek words for four and angle: four quarter turns in a row bring it back to where it started, and the cross-section of its cell is a square. Barium titanate below the Curie temperature has such a cell, with one side longer than the other two (CK, PDF p. 637), and the body-centred tetragonal cell is one of the three structures met in bearing steels (HK, PDF p. 307). A composite plate with equally many fibres in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) has the same symmetry: a quarter turn about the axis \(z\) puts the fibres along \(x\) onto the fibres along \(y\), and there are no fibres in the direction \(z\). The crystal shows the cause at the atoms, the plate shows the same property in a piece we can hold in the hand.

Definition 3.40 Tetragonal and cubic material (tetragonalen in kubičen material)

Let a material be orthotropic at the point \(P\) and let the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system with origin at \(P\) be the material axes. The material is tetragonal (tetragonalen) at \(P\) with respect to the axis \(z\) if it has the same elastic constants also in the system with the unit vectors of the axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), which we get by a quarter turn about the axis \(z\). A tetragonal material with respect to the axis \(x\) and with respect to the axis \(y\) is defined in the same way. The material is cubic (kubičen) at \(P\) if it is tetragonal with respect to each of the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\).

Source: LOVE §109 (PDF pp. 178-179), SADD §11.2.4 (PDF p. 337), BOWER §3.2.16 (PDF pp. 112-113). SADD describes cubic symmetry by orthotropy and a turn about the body diagonal of the cube, which exchanges the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) cyclically. That description gives the same three constants (checked with SymPy).

In the lectures these are the tetragonal and the cubic material (tetragonalno gradivo, kubično gradivo), and our transversely isotropic material is there the hexagonal material (heksagonalno gradivo), after the crystals with a hexagonal structure from the start of the section.

The definition assumes that the material is orthotropic. Why may we? The square net on the left equals its mirror image across the planes perpendicular to the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the one on the right across the plane perpendicular to the axis \(z\). The same holds for the plate with fibres.

When does the assumption fail? For crystals that are the same after a quarter turn about the axis \(z\) but have neither a mirror plane through the axis \(z\) nor an axis perpendicular to the axis \(z\) about which they are the same after a half turn. Let us draw such a crystal (figure 3.139). At the corners of a square net we place pinwheels with four curved arms. A quarter turn lays every pinwheel onto itself, while its mirror image across a plane through the axis \(z\) has the arms curved the other way. Why do we count the half turn too? The half turn about the axis \(x\) has the matrix \(\mat Q\) with the diagonal \(1\), \(-1\), \(-1\), the reversed axis \(x\) the matrix with the diagonal \(-1\), \(1\), \(1\). The matrices differ only by the factor \(-1\), which appears twice in \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\), so both rename the components of stress and strain in the same way, as in lemma 3.30. A crystal without both therefore in general has no planes of material symmetry in the axes of the net. What does it cost? We checked with SymPy that the quarter turn about the axis \(z\) alone leaves seven of the 21 constants of a symmetric matrix: besides the six we are about to get, also \(C_{16}\), with \(C_{26} = -C_{16}\). Among the tetragonal crystals LOVE lists four classes with six and three classes with seven constants (LOVE §109, PDF p. 179).

The seventh number, however, can be replaced by the angle by which the material axes are turned against the rows of atoms. We turn the axes about the axis \(z\) by the angle \(\theta\), so with \(c = \cos\theta\) and \(s = \sin\theta\), and compute with SymPy the element \(C_{16}\) in the new axes, which we plot over the angle \(\theta\) from \(0\) to \(45^\circ\):

\[\bar C_{16} = C_{16}\cos 4\theta - \tfrac14\,(C_{11} - C_{12} - 2C_{66})\sin 4\theta .\]

At \(\theta = 0\) this is \(C_{16}\), at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) it is \(-C_{16}\), because \(\cos 180^\circ = -1\) and \(\sin 180^\circ = 0\). The curve is continuous, so by the intermediate value theorem 2.79 it crosses zero in between, at the angle \(\theta_0\). In the axes turned by \(\theta_0\) all elements that (3.41) does not have are zero (SymPy). By lemma 3.30, written for this axis, the reversed axis \(\bar x\) changes the sign only of the components at places \(5\) and \(6\), which this form links only with the components at the same places, so the material keeps its constants also in such a system, and the same for the axis \(\bar y\). The planes perpendicular to the axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) are therefore planes of material symmetry, only they are not perpendicular to the rows of atoms. Our lemma therefore holds for all tetragonal crystals, for the classes with seven constants in the axes turned by \(\theta_0\). With the numbers of the figure, \(\theta_0 = 19{,}0^\circ\).

Lemma 3.41 Constants of a tetragonal material (konstante tetragonalnega materiala)

Let a material at the point \(P\) obey the generalized Hooke's law with a symmetric material stiffness matrix of the form (3.41). If the material is tetragonal with respect to the axis \(z\), then

\[C_{22} = C_{11} , \qquad C_{23} = C_{13} , \qquad C_{55} = C_{44} , \tag{3.46}\]

and the material has six constants, \(C_{11}\), \(C_{12}\), \(C_{13}\), \(C_{33}\), \(C_{44}\) and \(C_{66}\):

\[\mat C = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11} & C_{12} & C_{13} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ C_{12} & C_{11} & C_{13} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ C_{13} & C_{13} & C_{33} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{44} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{44} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{66} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{3.47}\]

Conversely, a material with the stiffness matrix (3.47) has the same constants in the system turned by a quarter turn about the axis \(z\).

Proof

We must show three equalities and the converse. Both follow from how the quarter turn renames the components (figure 3.133).

1. Three equalities.

  1. By step 2 of the first part of the proof of lemma 3.37, for the quarter turn about the axis \(z\)
    \[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} , \quad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} , \quad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} , \quad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} , \quad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} , \quad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]
    The turn exchanges the diagonal elements \(xx\) and \(yy\), leaves the element \(zz\), exchanges the elements of the column \(z\) and reverses the sign of one, and reverses the sign of the element \(xy\). The same holds for the strains, so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  2. Steps 3 to 6 of the same part of the proof use only this turn, the form (3.41) and the fact that the material has the same constants in the new axes. These are exactly our assumptions, so the steps hold here too and give \(C_{22} = C_{11}\), \(C_{23} = C_{13}\) and \(C_{55} = C_{44}\).
  3. The fourth equality of lemma 3.37, \(C_{66} = \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12})\), comes from the turn onto the diagonal. A tetragonal material need not have the same constants in the axes turned by \(45^\circ\), so we do not get it and \(C_{66}\) stays an independent constant.
  4. Of the nine constants in (3.41) the three equalities (3.46) express \(C_{22}\), \(C_{23}\) and \(C_{55}\) by the others. Six constants remain, the left pattern in figure 3.140.

2. The converse.

  1. Write the six equations \(\{\bar\sigma\} = \mat C\,\{\bar\varepsilon\}\) with the matrix (3.47) and the components in the new axes. We must show that they hold for every small strain. We put step 1 of the first part into them.
  2. The first equation, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{11}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{12}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{13}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), becomes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{12}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{11}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). This is the second row of (3.47) in the old axes. In the same way the second equation becomes the first row.
  3. The third equation, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = C_{13}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{13}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{33}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), becomes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + C_{13}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + C_{33}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), the third row.
  4. The fourth equation, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = C_{44}\,\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), becomes \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -C_{44}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), the fifth row. The fifth, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = C_{44}\,\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}}\), becomes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = C_{44}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}}\), the fourth row. The sixth, \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{66}\,\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), becomes \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -C_{66}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the sixth row.
  5. All six equations in the new axes are therefore the six rows of the law in the old axes, which by assumption hold for every small strain. There is only one matrix that gives the right stresses for every strain, since its column \(q\), multiplied by \(0{,}001\), is the column of stresses for the strain whose only nonzero element is \(0{,}001\) in place \(q\) (section 3.4.2). The material stiffness matrix in the new axes is therefore the same matrix (3.47).

Source: LOVE §109 (PDF p. 179) states the six constants without a derivation. The proof is not from the sources. We checked the equalities and the converse with SymPy.

What happens if the material is the same after a quarter turn about more than one axis? In a crystal with a cubic lattice \(c = a\), and the right view of figure 3.138 is then a square net like the left one.

Corollary 3.42 Stiffness matrix of a cubic material (togostna matrika kubičnega materiala)

Let a material at the point \(P\) obey the generalized Hooke's law with a symmetric material stiffness matrix of the form (3.41) and let it be tetragonal with respect to the axis \(z\) and with respect to the axis \(x\). Then

\[C_{11} = C_{22} = C_{33} , \qquad C_{12} = C_{13} = C_{23} , \qquad C_{44} = C_{55} = C_{66} ,\]

the material has three constants, \(C_{11}\), \(C_{12}\) and \(C_{44}\),

\[\mat C = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11} & C_{12} & C_{12} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ C_{12} & C_{11} & C_{12} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ C_{12} & C_{12} & C_{11} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{44} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{44} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & C_{44} \end{bmatrix} , \tag{3.48}\]

and it is tetragonal also with respect to the axis \(y\), hence cubic.

Proof

We must show six equalities and that the material is tetragonal with respect to the axis \(y\). We use lemma 3.41 on the constants of a tetragonal material for each axis separately.

  1. The material is tetragonal with respect to the axis \(z\), so by the lemma \(C_{22} = C_{11}\), \(C_{23} = C_{13}\) and \(C_{55} = C_{44}\).
  2. In the lemma the axis \(z\) has no special role. When the axis \(x\) takes the role of the axis \(z\), and the axes \(y\) and \(z\) the roles of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the places \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\), \(5\) and \(6\) map to the places \(2\), \(3\), \(1\), \(5\), \(6\) and \(4\), as in step 3 of the proof of corollary 3.39. The equalities (3.46) then become \(C_{33} = C_{22}\), \(C_{31} = C_{21}\) and \(C_{66} = C_{55}\). The matrix is symmetric, so the second equality is \(C_{13} = C_{12}\).
  3. Steps 1 and 2 give \(C_{11} = C_{22} = C_{33}\), then \(C_{23} = C_{13} = C_{12}\) and \(C_{44} = C_{55} = C_{66}\). Three constants remain, the right pattern in figure 3.140.
  4. When the axis \(y\) takes the role of the axis \(z\), and the axes \(z\) and \(x\) the roles of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), the places \(1\) to \(6\) map to the places \(3\), \(1\), \(2\), \(6\), \(4\) and \(5\), and the matrix (3.47) becomes a matrix with \(C_{11} = C_{33}\), \(C_{12} = C_{23}\) and \(C_{44} = C_{66}\). The matrix (3.48) has this form, so by the converse in the lemma the material has the same constants also after a quarter turn about the axis \(y\).

Source: SADD (11.2.13)-(11.2.14) (PDF p. 337), BOWER §3.2.16 (PDF pp. 112-113). The proof with two quarter turns is not from the sources. We checked the equalities with SymPy.

Each axis of a quarter turn took away three constants: of the nine the first left six, the second three, and the third took away nothing, because it already follows from the first two (figure 3.114, the right branch). A cubic material need not be isotropic. What it lacks is the fourth equality, \(C_{44} = \tfrac12\,(C_{11} - C_{12})\), which only the turn onto the diagonal gives.

Let us show with numbers on a tetragonal material how much this last equality means. Take a composite plate with equally many fibres in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) and choose for it the constants \(C_{11} = 60\) GPa, \(C_{12} = 5\) GPa, \(C_{13} = 4\) GPa, \(C_{33} = 12\) GPa, \(C_{44} = 3\) GPa and \(C_{66} = 4\) GPa. The numbers are ours, chosen for the example, not measured. From the plate we cut two squares of side 10 mm, one along the fibres and one at \(45^\circ\) to them, and stretch each by 10 µm in one direction so that its width and thickness do not change (figure 3.141).

The left square of side 10 mm has its fibres along the axes \(x\) and \(y\). We stretch it by 10 µm in the direction \(x\), so \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\) and all other components of strain are zero. The stresses are the first column of the matrix (3.47) times \(0{,}001\): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 60\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 5\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 4\) MPa perpendicular to the picture. We pull straight along half of the fibres, so the pull is large.

The right square has its fibres along the diagonals. Its sides point along the axes \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), turned by \(45^\circ\), with \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\), as in the second part of the proof of lemma 3.37. We stretch it by 10 µm in the direction \(\bar x\), so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\) and all other components in the new axes are zero. We know the matrix (3.47) only in the axes of the fibres, so we calculate in three steps.

  1. The strain in the axes of the fibres. In the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{a}} \sum_{\mathrm{b}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ab}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\) a single term remains, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = Q_{\mathrm{xi}}\,Q_{\mathrm{xj}} \cdot 0{,}001\). With \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1/\sqrt2\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}0005\), so \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}001\). For the fibres, the stretch along the diagonal is half as large a stretch in both directions and a shear between them.
  2. The stresses in the axes of the fibres. By (3.47), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = (60 + 5) \cdot 0{,}0005\) GPa \(= 32{,}5\) MPa, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = (4 + 4) \cdot 0{,}0005\) GPa \(= 4\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 4 \cdot 0{,}001\) GPa \(= 4\) MPa.
  3. The stresses in the axes of the square. From \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\) we get
    \[\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) + \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 36{,}5\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \bar\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) - \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 28{,}5\ \text{MPa} ,\]
    and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}) = 0\). These are the pull of 36,5 MPa and the transverse stress of 28,5 MPa.

For the same elongation the pull needed at \(45^\circ\) is \(60/36{,}5 = 1{,}64\) times smaller than along the fibres. Why? No fibre lies in the direction of the pull. By step 1 the fibres stretch only by \(0{,}0005\), half as much as the fibres along \(x\) on the left, which gives \(\tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}) = 32{,}5\) MPa. The rest of the deformation is shear between the fibres, as in a garden trellis of laths whose squares we pull into rhombi. Only the material between the fibres resists it, with the small \(C_{66} = 4\) GPa, which adds only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 4\) MPa. Why is the transverse stress so large, \(28{,}5\) MPa against \(5\) MPa on the left? A net pulled along its diagonal wants to narrow strongly, and we must hold its width by force.

What would the assumption cost that the plate is isotropic in its plane? Then the fourth equality would hold and \(C_{66}\) would be \(\tfrac12\,(60 - 5)\) GPa \(= 27{,}5\) GPa instead of \(4\) GPa. The calculation in three steps would give \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 27{,}5\) MPa and \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 32{,}5 + 27{,}5 = 60\) MPa, the same as along the fibres, so \(1{,}64\) times too much. A tetragonal material is the same in two directions, not in all. In the axes turned by \(45^\circ\) it again has the pattern of six constants, but with other numbers: NumPy gives \(\bar C_{11} = 36{,}5\) GPa, \(\bar C_{12} = 28{,}5\) GPa and \(\bar C_{66} = 27{,}5\) GPa, the other three constants are the same.

An example of a cubic material is a copper crystal, which has its atoms arranged in a cubic lattice (BOWER §3.2.16, PDF pp. 112-114). Figure 3.142 shows on the left one face of such a lattice: the atoms lie in rows along the axes \(x\) and \(y\), which point along the edges of the cube, and neighbouring atoms in a row are \(a\) apart. The planes perpendicular to the edges of the cube are planes of material symmetry, and the lattice is the same also after a turn by a quarter revolution about each edge, since the turn lays the rows along \(x\) onto the rows along \(y\). After the turn that puts the axes onto the diagonals of a face of the cube, however, the lattice is not the same: along the new axis the neighbouring atoms are \(a\sqrt2\) apart, not \(a\). By corollary 3.42, three constants remain (SADD (11.2.14), PDF p. 337). For copper \(C_{11} = 168{,}4\) GPa, \(C_{12} = 121{,}4\) GPa and \(C_{44} = 75{,}4\) GPa (BOWER Table 3.5, PDF p. 115). If the crystal were isotropic, we would have \(C_{44} = \tfrac12\,(168{,}4 - 121{,}4)\) GPa \(= 23{,}5\) GPa. The real \(C_{44}\) is \(75{,}4/23{,}5 = 3{,}21\) times larger, as the lengths of the two bars on the right of the figure show. A copper crystal resists shear along the faces of its cube more than three times as strongly as an isotropic material with the same \(C_{11}\) and \(C_{12}\) would. BOWER uses exactly this ratio, \(2C_{44}/(C_{11} - C_{12})\), as a measure of anisotropy (BOWER, PDF p. 114).

Why then do we treat copper and steel in everyday pieces as isotropic? A piece of metal consists of very many tiny crystals, grains, with differently oriented lattices, as we said in section 3.1 and drew in figure 3.36, and most such metals behave isotropically (SADD, PDF p. 92, BOWER §3.2.1, PDF p. 96). When a sheet is rolled, however, the grains become similarly oriented (BOWER, PDF p. 193), and then the piece of metal is anisotropic too (BOWER, PDF p. 103).

3.4.6 The short route to the isotropic law

We reached the matrix (3.40) by a long route, from 21 constants through planes of symmetry and turns. That route shows which symmetry takes away which constants. There is another view, which tells something else: why Hooke's law of an isotropic material (3.28) has exactly the form in which the stress is a multiple of the identity matrix plus a multiple of the strain. An isotropic material has no special direction. Its constants can therefore be built only from something that itself has no special direction, that is, something that has the same components in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems. We know one such example from section 2.9.7. The matrix \(-p\,\mat I\) of the stress in a fluid at rest has the same components in every system, because the pressure is the same in all directions.

Definition 3.43 Isotropic second-order tensor (izotropni tenzor drugega reda)

A second-order tensor is isotropic (izotropen) if it has the same components in all rectangular Cartesian coordinate systems with the same unit of length. For its matrix \(\mat A\) in one such system this means, by the rule (2.64), that \(\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T = \mat A\) for every rotation matrix \(\mat Q\).

Source: CM §2.5.4 (PDF p. 87), SADD §1.5 (PDF p. 18).

The word isotropic means the same here as for a material, the same in all directions, only that we now say it of a quantity and not of a substance. In section 2.9.7 we quoted that every such tensor is a multiple of the identity matrix, and left the claim without proof. Let us prove it. Two turns by a quarter revolution suffice, the first about the axis \(z\) and the second about the axis \(x\). We drew the first in figure 3.133. The table in the new axes has the same elements as the table in the old ones, only moved and some with a reversed sign. A matrix that is to be the same in both systems must therefore have equal numbers in the cells that are exchanged, and a number that equals its own opposite is zero.

Figure 3.143 shows where the proof is going. The grid has three rows and three columns, \(\mat A\) names the matrix, and the columns and the rows are labelled \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) (the row \(z\) is at the bottom, the column \(z\) on the right). The three diagonal fields will be the same number \(a\). The turn about the axis \(z\) ties \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\) to \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and the turn about the axis \(x\) ties \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\) to \(A_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The six fields off the diagonal will be zero, in three groups: the column \(z\), the row \(z\) and the pair \(A_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

Lemma 3.44 The only isotropic second-order tensor (edini izotropni tenzor drugega reda)

Let \(\mat A\) be a matrix of size \(3 \times 3\) with real elements \(A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The following two statements are equivalent.

  1. For every rotation matrix \(\mat Q\), \(\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T = \mat A\).
  2. There is a real number \(a\) such that \(\mat A = a\,\mat I\), where \(\mat I\) is the identity matrix.

A second-order tensor is therefore isotropic exactly when its matrix is a multiple of the identity matrix.

Proof

We have to show that statement 1 implies statement 2 and statement 2 implies statement 1.

1 implies 2.

  1. Take the turn by a quarter revolution about the axis \(z\), for which \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) (the new axes in figure 3.133). The rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are these three vectors (definition 2.44), so its nonzero elements are \(Q_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yx}} = -1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1\).
  2. The element of the matrix \(\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T\) in the row \(a\) and the column \(b\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\mathrm{ai}}\,A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,Q_{\mathrm{bj}}\). Each row of \(\mat Q\) has a single nonzero element, so each double sum has a single term. We get the right table of figure 3.133:
    \[\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{yy}} & -A_{\mathrm{yx}} & A_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ -A_{\mathrm{xy}} & A_{\mathrm{xx}} & -A_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ A_{\mathrm{zy}} & -A_{\mathrm{zx}} & A_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} .\]
  3. By statement 1 this matrix equals \(\mat A\), element by element. The diagonal elements give \(A_{\mathrm{yy}} = A_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  4. The elements of the column \(z\) give \(A_{\mathrm{yz}} = A_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(-A_{\mathrm{xz}} = A_{\mathrm{yz}}\). From the two it follows that \(A_{\mathrm{xz}} = -A_{\mathrm{xz}}\), so \(2A_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\), hence \(A_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\).
  5. The elements of the row \(z\) give \(A_{\mathrm{zy}} = A_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(-A_{\mathrm{zx}} = A_{\mathrm{zy}}\), so in the same way \(A_{\mathrm{zx}} = 0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\).
  1. Take also the turn by a quarter revolution about the axis \(x\), for which \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The old axes \(y\) and \(z\) are blackwhite on the left, the new ones blue. The nonzero elements of the matrix \(\mat Q\) are now \(Q_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\), \(Q_{\mathrm{yz}} = 1\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{zy}} = -1\), and as in step 2 we get from the left table the right one:
    \[\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{xx}} & A_{\mathrm{xz}} & -A_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ A_{\mathrm{zx}} & A_{\mathrm{zz}} & -A_{\mathrm{zy}} \\ -A_{\mathrm{yx}} & -A_{\mathrm{yz}} & A_{\mathrm{yy}} \end{bmatrix} .\]
  2. By statement 1 this matrix equals \(\mat A\) too. The element in the row \(y\) and the column \(y\) gives \(A_{\mathrm{zz}} = A_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The element in the row \(x\) and the column \(y\) gives \(A_{\mathrm{xy}} = A_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which is zero by step 4. The element in the row \(y\) and the column \(x\) gives \(A_{\mathrm{yx}} = A_{\mathrm{zx}}\), which is zero by step 5.
  3. All six elements off the diagonal are therefore zero, and by steps 3 and 7, \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} = A_{\mathrm{yy}} = A_{\mathrm{zz}}\). With the number \(a = A_{\mathrm{xx}}\) we have \(\mat A = a\,\mat I\) (definition 1.108).

2 implies 1.

  1. Let \(\mat A = a\,\mat I\) and let \(\mat Q\) be a rotation matrix. We take the number \(a\) out, and the product with the identity matrix does not change a matrix, so \(\mat Q\,(a\,\mat I)\,\mat Q^\T = a\,\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T\).
  2. A rotation matrix is orthogonal (lemma 2.47 on the orthogonality of the rotation matrix), so by (2.52) \(\mat Q\,\mat Q^\T = \mat I\), and \(\mat Q\,\mat A\,\mat Q^\T = a\,\mat I = \mat A\).

Source: CM (PDF p. 87) states the claim without proof, SADD §1.5 (PDF p. 18) states only that the identity matrix is isotropic. The proof by two quarter turns is not from the sources. We checked the matrices in steps 2 and 6 with SymPy.

Statement 1 demands equality under every turn, and the proof used only two. A matrix that has the same components already in these two turned systems therefore has them in all. A single turn does not suffice. Take the matrix with the diagonal \(1\), \(1\), \(2\) and zeros elsewhere. Multiplied by \(0{,}001\), it is the strain of a piece that stretches twice as much in the direction \(z\) as in the directions \(x\) and \(y\) (figure 3.145).

On the left we look at the piece along the axis \(z\). The square with a circle drawn in it is grey and dashed before the strain, orange after it. From the centre we draw three fibres, along the axis \(x\), along the axis \(y\) and along the diagonal between them. Each gets longer by an equally long blue piece, which belongs to the number \(1\) on the diagonal of the matrix, so the circle stays a circle. The new axes of the turn about the axis \(z\) therefore see the same, \(\bar A_{\mathrm{xx}} = \bar A_{\mathrm{yy}} = 1\), and so it is for every angle of a turn about the axis \(z\), since every fibre in the plane \(xy\) gets equally longer. On the right we look along the axis \(x\). The fibre along the axis \(z\) gets longer by a blue piece twice as long as the fibre along the axis \(y\), and the circle becomes an ellipse, elongated along the axis \(z\). Under the turn of step 6 the new axis \(\bar y\) points along the old axis \(z\), so \(\bar A_{\mathrm{yy}} = A_{\mathrm{zz}} = 2\) and not \(1\). The elements \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are swapped, just as \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\) are swapped under the turn about the axis \(z\), and the matrix is no longer the same. The axis \(z\) is a special direction for this piece, and only a turn that moves this axis notices it.

We have met the lemma twice in the book without stating it. The stress in a fluid at rest is \(-p\,\mat I\), and the strain of an isotropic material due to temperature is \(\alpha\,\Delta T\,\mat I\), under which a piece keeps its shape (section 3.3, figure 3.89). Neither quantity may be different in one direction than in the others, so a single number describes each.

The elastic constants have four indices, so the identity matrix alone is not enough for them. But from it we can build numbers with four indices. We denote the element of the identity matrix in the row \(i\) and the column \(j\) by \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). This is the Kronecker delta of chapter 2 (definition 2.58): \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1\) when the indices are equal and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) when they differ. A product of two deltas ties the four indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(l\) into two pairs, and this can be done in three ways (figure 3.146).

In the first column \(i\) is tied to \(j\) and \(k\) to \(l\), this is the product \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\). In the second \(i\) is tied to \(k\) and \(j\) to \(l\), the product \(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\). In the third \(i\) is tied to \(l\) and \(j\) to \(k\), the product \(\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\). There is no fourth way, because the index \(i\) has only three possible partners. Each product is \(1\) when the indices in both pairs are equal, and \(0\) otherwise. The tables under them hold the strain components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\), the row belongs to the index \(k\) and the column to the index \(l\). When we multiply a product of deltas by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) and sum over \(k\) and \(l\), it acts as a sieve that multiplies most of the nine terms by zero. For \(i = j\) the first product keeps the diagonal, where \(k = l\), while for \(i \neq j\) we have \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) and it keeps nothing. The second keeps a single cell with \(k = i\) and \(l = j\), the third the cell with \(k = j\) and \(l = i\). Under the tables is written what is left of the sum.

CM and SADD state that sums of multiples of these three products are the only numbers with four indices that are the same in all turned systems, if they change by the rule with one factor \(Q\) for each index from section 2.9.7 (CM (2.5.24), PDF p. 87, SADD (4.2.6), PDF p. 93). They do not write down a proof, and SADD refers to another book. We do not need this claim, because we already know the stiffness matrix of an isotropic material from corollary 3.39. We only have to show that the three products write it down.

Figure 3.147 shows in advance how we shall divide the 36 places in the grid, six by six. The numbers at the edge from 1 to 6 are the indices of row and column. The three places on the diagonal of the normals get \(\lambda + 2\mu\). The six places off the diagonal of the normals get \(\lambda\). The three places on the diagonal of the shears get \(\mu\). The remaining 24 places are zero: the 18 places where a normal pair meets a shear and the six places where two different shears meet.

Lemma 3.45 Isotropic elastic constants written with deltas (izotropne elastične konstante z deltami)

Let the material at the point \(P\) satisfy the generalized Hooke's law with constants for which \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}} = C_{\mathrm{ijlk}}\), and let its material stiffness matrix be the matrix (3.40) with the Lamé constants \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\). Then for all indices \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) and \(l\) running over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\),

\[C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = \lambda\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} + \mu\,(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}} + \delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}) , \tag{3.49}\]

where \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the element of the identity matrix, \(1\) for \(i = j\) and \(0\) for \(i \neq j\).

Proof

We have to show that the right-hand side, call it \(D_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\), gives for each of the 81 quadruples of indices the constant that the matrix (3.40) fixes at that place. We sort the quadruples by which indices are equal, and in this way the places of the matrix fall into five groups.

  1. Swapping the indices in a pair. The left column of figure 3.148 holds the three products, drawn with arcs as in figure 3.146. In the middle column we swap the letters \(i\) and \(j\), while the arcs stay where they were, since they tie the places of the indices and not the letters. This gives \(D_{\mathrm{jikl}}\). In the right column we put the letters back in the order \(i\), \(j\), \(k\), \(l\) and carry the arcs with the letters. The first product stays the same, because \(\delta_{\mathrm{ji}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the second becomes the third and the third the second. Both carry the same number \(\mu\), so the sum does not change. The same holds for swapping \(k\) and \(l\). So \(D_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = D_{\mathrm{jikl}} = D_{\mathrm{ijlk}}\), as holds for the constants. It is therefore enough to check one order in each pair, that is the \(6 \cdot 6 = 36\) places of the material stiffness matrix (definition 3.27).
  2. Normal with the same normal, \(i = j = k = l\), for example \(xxxx\). All three products are \(1\), so \(D_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = \lambda + 2\mu\). This is \(C_{11}\), and likewise \(C_{22}\) and \(C_{33}\). There are \(3\) such places.
  3. Normal with another normal, \(i = j\), \(k = l\) and \(i \neq k\), for example \(xxyy\). The first product is \(1\). In the second \(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}} = \delta_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), in the third \(\delta_{\mathrm{il}} = \delta_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). So \(D_{\mathrm{xxyy}} = \lambda\). This is \(C_{12}\), and likewise all \(6\) places off the diagonal in the upper left part of the matrix.
  4. Shear with the same shear, \(i \neq j\), \(k = i\) and \(l = j\), for example \(yzyz\). The first product is zero, because \(\delta_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0\). The second is \(\delta_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1\). The third is \(\delta_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\). So \(D_{\mathrm{yzyz}} = \mu\). This is \(C_{44}\), and likewise \(C_{55}\) and \(C_{66}\). There are \(3\) such places.
  5. Normal with shear, \(i = j\) and \(k \neq l\), for example \(xxyz\). The first product is zero, because \(\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} = 0\). The second product \(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\) would be \(1\) only for \(k = i\) and \(l = i\), that is for \(k = l\), which does not hold here. The third product \(\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\) has the same two factors. So \(D_{\mathrm{xxyz}} = 0\), like \(C_{14}\). In the same way it is zero for \(i \neq j\) and \(k = l\). There are \(9 + 9 = 18\) such places.
  6. Shear with another shear, \(i \neq j\), \(k \neq l\), and the pair \(kl\) is neither \(ij\) nor \(ji\), for example \(yzxz\). The first product is zero. The second would be \(1\) only for \(k = i\) and \(l = j\), the third only for \(l = i\) and \(k = j\). So \(D_{\mathrm{yzxz}} = 0\), like \(C_{45}\). There are \(6\) such places.
  7. Steps 2 to 6 cover \(3 + 6 + 3 + 18 + 6 = 36\) places, all the places of the matrix, and at each of them \(D_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) equals the element of the matrix (3.40), the last pattern in figure 3.136. By step 1 the equality holds for all 81 quadruples.

Source: CM (2.5.24) (PDF p. 87) and (6.3.30) (PDF p. 266), SADD (4.2.6) (PDF p. 93). In (6.3.31) CM merges the two terms with \(\mu\) into \(2\mu\,\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\). For a symmetric strain this gives the same stresses, but it is not symmetric in the first pair of indices, so for the individual constants we take the form (2.5.24) without its last term. The check place by place is not from the sources. We checked all 81 values with SymPy: 21 are nonzero, three are \(\lambda + 2\mu\), six \(\lambda\) and twelve \(\mu\).

Why does the third product have the same number \(\mu\) as the second? SADD writes the general form with three independent numbers, \(\alpha\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} + \beta\,\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}} + \gamma\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\) (SADD (4.2.6), PDF p. 93).
