The second and the third product pick \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}}\) out of the strain (the second and the third sieve in figure 3.146), which are the same number because the strain is symmetric. So only the sum \(\beta + \gamma\) enters the stress, just as in lemma 3.26 on swapping the indices within a pair the material fixes only the sum \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} + C_{\mathrm{ijlk}}\). The sum \(\beta + \gamma\) is the number in front of the strain in the law (3.28), that is \(2\mu\). By the agreement of that lemma we split the sum into two equal parts, and each is \(\mu\). In the lectures the constant is written as \(\lambda\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}} + \alpha\,\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}} + \beta\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\) with \(\alpha + \beta = 2\mu\), which is the same sum with other letters.

Now we get Hooke's law of an isotropic material in five lines. We stand at the point \(P\) of the material of lemma 3.45. The strain is small, as the generalized Hooke's law demands, so it is described by the small strain tensor, which is symmetric already by definition 1.121. We put (3.49) into the generalized Hooke's law (3.37). The numbers \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) do not depend on \(k\) and \(l\), so we take them out of the sums, and the double sum falls into three, one for each column of figure 3.146:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} + \mu \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} + \mu \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} .\]
\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} + \mu\,\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} + \mu\,\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} .\]

In the first sum \(\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\) is zero except for \(l = k\). Of the nine terms the three on the diagonal remain, and the sum is the trace of the strain matrix:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tr\ten\varepsilon .\]
\[\delta_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}} = \tr\ten\varepsilon .\]

In the second sum \(\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\) is zero except for \(k = i\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\) is zero except for \(l = j\). A single term remains:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]
\[\delta_{\mathrm{ik}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

In the third sum the term with \(l = i\) and \(k = j\) remains, for \(i \neq j\) the cell on the other side of the diagonal, for \(i = j\) the same cell as in the second sum. The strain is symmetric (definition 1.121), so this is the same number:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]
\[\delta_{\mathrm{il}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{jk}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ji}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]

We add all three sums:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.50}\]
\[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kk}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} . \tag{3.50}\]

This is Hooke's law (3.28) written in components, since \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the element of the matrix \(\mat I\) in the row \(i\) and the column \(j\) (SADD (4.2.7), PDF p. 93). The first term is nonzero only for \(i = j\), so the trace contributes only to the normal stresses. The number \(2\) in front of \(\mu\) is the sum of the second and the third sieve.

Let us test the lines on steel with \(\lambda = 113{,}1\) GPa and \(\mu = 75{,}38\) GPa from section 3.4.2. The strain matrix has the labels \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) at the edge and the values in its fields. Let the strain have \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = 0{,}0005\), and all other components zero. Its trace is \(0{,}001\), since of the three diagonal cells only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is nonzero.

  1. For \(i = j = x\) all three sieves are open. The first gives \(\lambda \cdot 0{,}001\), the second and the third each \(\mu \cdot 0{,}001\), together \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = (\lambda + 2\mu) \cdot 0{,}001 = 263{,}8\) MPa, as in section 3.4.2.
  2. For \(i = j = y\) the first sieve gives \(113{,}1\) MPa and the other two give zero, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\). So \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 113{,}1\) MPa, and likewise \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\).
  3. For \(i = x\) and \(j = y\) the first sieve is closed, because \(\delta_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The second gives \(\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 75{,}38\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}0005 = 37{,}69\) MPa, the third \(\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = 37{,}69\) MPa. Together \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 75{,}38\) MPa.

We get the same if we put all 81 constants (3.49) into (3.37) and add nine terms for each stress (checked with SymPy). The third line shows where the \(2\mu\) in shear comes from: the shear component of the strain enters the sum twice, as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) and as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

What has this view added? The long route showed which symmetry of the material takes away which constants, and it also treated materials that are not isotropic. The short route shows why the isotropic law has exactly two terms: from the identity matrix and the strain we can build, without a special direction, only two expressions linear in the strain, the trace times the identity matrix and the strain itself. Linearity is demanded by the generalized Hooke's law (3.37), in which the stress is a sum of constants multiplied by the strain components. Without this demand the expression \((\tr\ten\varepsilon)^2\,\mat I\), for example, would also have no special direction. It is short because it leaves the harder part to the claim that there are no other isotropic numbers with four indices. We did not prove that claim, and we did not use it either: that the three products suffice we know from corollary 3.39.

3.4.7 A strip of composite

Let us return to the composite from the beginning of the section. A thin plate of carbon fibres in epoxy resin lies in the plane \(xy\), the axis \(z\) is perpendicular to it, and all fibres are parallel and point in the direction of the axis \(x\) (figure 3.106, right). We treat the material as orthotropic with the material axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), like the left cube of figure 3.117. The constants are \(E_{\mathrm{x}} = 205\) GPa, \(E_{\mathrm{y}} = 10\) GPa, \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0{,}26\) and \(G_{\mathrm{xy}} = 6\) GPa (SADD Table 11.2, PDF p. 341, where direction \(1\) is the fibre direction and the shear modulus is \(\mu_{12}\)). SADD gives only \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\). We get the number \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\) from the reciprocal relation (3.43): \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}} = \nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,E_{\mathrm{y}}/E_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}26 \cdot 10/205 = 0{,}01268\).

The plate is thin and loaded only in its own plane. There are no forces on its large faces, so there \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero, and because the plate is thin we assume that they are zero everywhere in it (SADD §7.2, PDF p. 152). This is the plane stress of section 3.2.9. The assumption holds for a plate whose thickness is small compared with its other dimensions, if no force acts on it in the direction \(z\) and the load does not vary through the thickness (SADD §7.2, PDF p. 152). In general it is an approximation (SADD, PDF p. 154). In our case it costs nothing: the stress will be the same throughout the strip, and the components that are zero on the large faces are then zero everywhere. From (3.42) we then need only the rows for \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), in which only the columns for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) remain:

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} - \frac{\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}}{E_{\mathrm{y}}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} , \qquad \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}}{G_{\mathrm{xy}}} . \tag{3.51}\]

The strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is not zero, but for the plane of the plate we do not need it, and so we do not need \(\nu_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{yz}}\) either.

From the plate we cut a long narrow strip of length \(L\) and width \(b\) and pull it by its ends, like the bar in chapter 2. Let the force be distributed evenly over the ends and cause the stress \(\sigma = 10\) MPa along the strip. This is an idealization, as for the bar. The real grips of a testing machine hold the ends differently, which changes the stresses near the ends but not farther from them (SADD §5.6, PDF pp. 114-115). The numbers below therefore hold for the middle part of a long strip. For a composite the region near the ends where the stresses differ can be several times longer than for an isotropic material, since end effects in anisotropic materials decay much more slowly (SADD, PDF pp. 114-115). The strip must therefore be correspondingly longer. The stress \(10\) MPa is small, all strains will be at most \(0{,}001\) in size. We write stresses and moduli in megapascals, \(E_{\mathrm{x}} = 205\,000\) MPa, \(E_{\mathrm{y}} = 10\,000\) MPa and \(G_{\mathrm{xy}} = 6\,000\) MPa.

The figure shows two such strips of length \(L\) and width \(b\). At the top is the strip cut along the fibres, at the bottom the strip cut across them, both drawn grey dashed, as they are before loading. Each has its own material axes, the axis \(x\) always along the fibres: at the top it points along the strip, at the bottom across it. We pull both with the same stress \(\sigma\) (the arrows at the top and at the bottom). The strips after loading are orange (top, bottom). They are drawn so that the left end stays in place and the whole elongation shows at the right end. Strains are exaggerated 300 times, otherwise the orange outline could not be told from the grey one.

Along the fibres. The strip points in the direction \(x\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 10\) MPa and the other two stresses are zero. By (3.51), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 10/205\,000 = 4{,}878 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -0{,}26 \cdot 4{,}878 \cdot 10^{-5} = -1{,}268 \cdot 10^{-5}\). So the strip lengthens by \(4{,}878 \cdot 10^{-5}\,L\) and narrows by \(1{,}268 \cdot 10^{-5}\,b\).

Across the fibres. The strip points in the direction \(y\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = 10\) MPa. Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = 10/10\,000 = 1{,}000 \cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}01268 \cdot 10/10\,000 = -1{,}268 \cdot 10^{-5}\). This strip lengthens by \(1{,}000 \cdot 10^{-3}\,L\), and in the direction of the fibres it narrows by \(1{,}268 \cdot 10^{-5}\,b\).

The strip across the fibres stretches \(20{,}5\) times more (the lower elongation against the upper one). At the same stress the stretch is \(\sigma/E\), and the ratio of the moduli is \(E_{\mathrm{x}}/E_{\mathrm{y}} = 205/10 = 20{,}5\). The lateral strains, however, are equal in both cases, \(-1{,}268 \cdot 10^{-5}\) (top, bottom). This is no coincidence. When pulled along the fibres the lateral strain is \(-\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), when pulled across them \(-\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\sigma/E_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the reciprocal relation says that the fractions \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}}\) are equal. When pulled across the fibres the strip contracts along the fibres by only \(0{,}01268\) of its stretch. Why so little? By the reciprocal relation this contraction equals the contraction \(\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma/E_{\mathrm{x}}\) when pulled along the fibres, and that is small because \(E_{\mathrm{x}}\) is large. The stiff fibres resist contraction just as they resist stretching.

Obliquely. What about a strip cut obliquely to the fibres? Let its length point in the direction of the unit vector \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\) with \(c = 4/5 = 0{,}8\) and \(s = 3/5 = 0{,}6\), and the direction across it be \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-s, c, 0)\), as for turned axes in section 2.9. The numbers satisfy \(c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}64 + 0{,}36 = 1\) (figure 3.151). The direction is shown by the triangle with sides \(0{,}8\), \(0{,}6\) and \(1\): for every unit of length along the strip we move \(0{,}8\) in the direction of the fibres and \(0{,}6\) across them. We pull the strip with the stress \(\sigma = 10\) MPa along \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\).

The figure shows, grey dashed, the strip of length \(L\) before loading. The fibres point in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the material (the material axes are at the upper left) and the axes of the strip \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) are on the right. We pull the strip along its length, in the direction \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\). Orange is the strip after loading, drawn in advance from the numbers we compute in the five steps below: it lengthens and its end tilts, so that the rectangle becomes a parallelogram. The middle of the left end is drawn in place, strains are exaggerated 400 times.

We know the constants of the material only in the material axes, so the computation runs in them. In thought we cut from the strip a small rectangle with sides along the material axes (figure 3.152).

On the left is the rectangle with the fibres along its longer side. We chose the sides in the ratio \(4 : 3\) because then the diagonal of length \(5a\) points exactly along the strip, in the direction \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\): \(4a/5a = 0{,}8 = c\) and \(3a/5a = 0{,}6 = s\). The length \(a\) is any small length. The material axes are at the lower left. The arrows and the right part of the figure are explained in the steps.

  1. Stresses in the material axes. In a bar pulled by an axial stress \(\sigma\), the traction vector on the face with the unit normal \(\vek n\) is \(\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) if the axis \(x\) points along the bar (section 2.6.6). The number \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the projection of the normal onto the direction of the bar, so in a form not tied to the axes \(\vek t(\vek n) = \sigma\,(\vek n\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}})\,\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\). For \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) we have \(\vek n\cdot\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = c\), for \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) it is \(s\). Therefore on the right face \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \sigma c\,(c, s, 0)\) and on the top face \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = \sigma s\,(c, s, 0)\). Both arrows point along the strip, because we pull the strip only along itself. Their components in the figure are \(6{,}4\), \(3{,}6\) and on both faces \(4{,}8\) MPa. So in its own axes the material feels, besides two tensions, a shear as well, although we only pull the strip. By definition 2.27
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma c^2 = 6{,}4\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma s^2 = 3{,}6\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma c s = 4{,}8\ \text{MPa} .\]
  2. Strains in the material axes by (3.51). The right part of figure 3.152 shows them on the rectangle before the deformation and after it: along the fibres it hardly stretches, across them it stretches about \(13\) times more, and most is done by the shear, in which the layers slide past one another along the fibres. The shear is drawn as sliding of the layers, as for the sheared cube in section 1.6.2. It differs from a shear without rotation only by a small rotation of the whole rectangle, which changes no length. The numbers are
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{6{,}4}{205\,000} - 0{,}01268 \cdot \frac{3{,}6}{10\,000} = 3{,}122 \cdot 10^{-5} - 0{,}457 \cdot 10^{-5} = 2{,}665 \cdot 10^{-5} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} &= -0{,}26 \cdot \frac{6{,}4}{205\,000} + \frac{3{,}6}{10\,000} = -0{,}081 \cdot 10^{-4} + 3{,}600 \cdot 10^{-4} = 3{,}519 \cdot 10^{-4} , \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac{4{,}8}{6\,000} = 8{,}000 \cdot 10^{-4} . \end{aligned}\]
  3. Strain along the strip. An imagined short fibre in the sense of definition 1.25 that points in the direction \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) has, by (1.61), the strain \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,c^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,s^2 + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,c s = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,c^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,s^2 + \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,c s\), since \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) has component \(z\) equal to zero. In the figure this is the diagonal \(AC\). The corner \(C\) moves to \(C'\): in the direction of the fibres by \(4a\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + 3a\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) (the stretch and the slide), across them by \(3a\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The diagonal lengthens by the projection of this displacement onto its own direction, \(5a\,\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c\,(4a\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + 3a\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}) + s \cdot 3a\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The part of the displacement perpendicular to the diagonal turns it by the angle \(1{,}319 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and lengthens it by only half the square of this angle, \(8{,}7 \cdot 10^{-9}\) of its length, about \(60\,000\) times less than the stretch below, so we neglect this part. Dividing by \(5a\) and using \(4/5 = c\) and \(3/5 = s\) gives the same sum of three terms. The numbers give
    \[\begin{aligned} \bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 2{,}665 \cdot 10^{-5} \cdot 0{,}64 + 3{,}519 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 0{,}36 + 8{,}000 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 0{,}48 \\ &= (0{,}1706 + 1{,}2668 + 3{,}8400) \cdot 10^{-4} = 5{,}277 \cdot 10^{-4} . \end{aligned}\]
  4. Shear between the directions of the strip. This is the angle by which the end of the strip tilts towards its length. By lemma 2.55 with the rows \((c, s, 0)\) and \((-s, c, 0)\) of the matrix \(\mat Q\), \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -cs\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + cs\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + (c^2 - s^2)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so
    \[\begin{aligned} \bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= 2cs\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}) + (c^2 - s^2)\,\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ &= 0{,}96 \cdot 3{,}252 \cdot 10^{-4} + 0{,}28 \cdot 8{,}000 \cdot 10^{-4} = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4} . \end{aligned}\]
  5. So the strip lengthens by \(5{,}277 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of its length. The modulus in the direction of the strip is the ratio of the stress to the strain along the strip, \(\bar E = \sigma/\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 10/(5{,}277 \cdot 10^{-4})\) MPa \(= 18\,950\) MPa \(= 18{,}95\) GPa.

The oblique strip is much closer to the strip across the fibres than to the strip along them: its modulus \(18{,}95\) GPa is only \(1{,}9\) times \(10\) GPa, but \(10{,}8\) times less than \(205\) GPa. Moreover, it shears. The shear \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}\) is even slightly larger than the stretch \(5{,}277 \cdot 10^{-4}\), and the rectangular strip becomes a parallelogram. An isotropic strip does not shear when pulled. Its constants are the same in the axes of the strip as in any other axes, and in the matrix (3.40) the normal stresses are not related to shear. An orthotropic material pulled obliquely to the material axes thus behaves like a monoclinic one (CM, PDF p. 267). Where does so much compliance come from? The largest contribution in step 3 is \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,cs = 3{,}840 \cdot 10^{-4}\), from the shear in the material axes, almost three quarters of the whole stretch \(5{,}277 \cdot 10^{-4}\). In figure 3.152 this is the sliding of the layers, which carries the corner \(C\) far along the fibres. Under the shear \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) the length in the direction \(x\) does not change, since the strain in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which stays zero under shear alone. In the figure the fibres after the deformation stay almost as long as before and only slide past one another. The stiff fibres therefore do not resist the shear, and the shear modulus \(G_{\mathrm{xy}} = 6\) GPa is the smallest of the constants of the plate.

In computing the modulus \(18{,}95\) GPa we assumed that the strip carries only the tension \(\sigma\) along itself everywhere, that is, that its ends are free to tilt. In figure 3.153 the strip is drawn horizontally, before loading and in both cases pulled with the stress \(\sigma\). At the top the ends tilt freely by the angle \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}\), as in figure 3.151. The grips at the bottom hold the ends perpendicular to the direction of the pull and on its line, so they must turn each end back by this angle. Turning needs a moment at each end, and both moments have the same sense. For the strip to be in equilibrium, they are balanced by the moment of two opposite transverse forces at the ends. The strip therefore bends along its whole length, not only near the ends. The piece of the strip between the left grip and any cross-section is in equilibrium only if the cross-section carries the moment of the grip reduced by the moment of the transverse force about the cross-section, and this difference is zero only in the middle. The stress from this bending is the smaller, the longer the strip is compared to its width \(b\), since the same angle \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is undone gradually over a longer length. The modulus \(18{,}95\) GPa therefore holds for a strip whose ends are free to tilt, and for a strip in grips only approximately, the better, the longer the strip.

The oblique strip also shows what the definition of a plane of symmetry rejects. A cube with fibres in the direction \(x\) has the same constants when the axis \(y\) is reversed (figure 3.117, left), while inclined fibres spoil this plane (right). Now we have numbers for it. For pure tension along the strip we are interested in the constant that connects the normal stress along the strip with the shear, \(k = \bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The plane perpendicular to the axis \(\bar y\) of the strip is not a plane of symmetry if this constant has a different value in the system with the axis \(\bar y\) reversed than in the original one. We check in three steps in figure 3.154.

  1. In the original system (the axes of the strip), by step 4, at \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma = 10\) MPa (the pull on the strip) the shear is \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}\): by this much the right angle between the directions \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) decreases. So \(k = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}/10\ \text{MPa} = 5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{MPa}^{-1}\).
  2. When we reverse the axis \(\bar y\), \(\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not change (the pull), since it has no index \(\bar y\). The strip tilts as before, only the axis \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) points the other way. The shear \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) has one such index and by the same reasoning as for the axis \(z\) it changes sign, \(-5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}\): the angle between the directions \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) now increases by \(5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-4}\).
  3. In the reversed system we therefore have \(k = -5{,}362 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{MPa}^{-1}\). The constants are different, and the plane perpendicular to \(\bar y\) is not a plane of symmetry. The same reasoning holds for the axis \(\bar x\).

If the constants were equal, \(k = -k\) would give \(k = 0\). This holds for the cube with fibres in the direction \(x\), which does not connect tension along the fibres with shear, so there the plane perpendicular to \(y\) has this property. For the strip \(k \ne 0\). What remains is the plane perpendicular to the axis \(z\), since in the axes of the material the material has a plane of symmetry perpendicular to \(z\), and the axis \(z\) is the same in both systems.

How does the modulus depend on the direction of the strip? Let us repeat steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 with general numbers \(c\) and \(s\) and the stress \(\sigma\).

  1. By step 1, the components of the traction vectors are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma c^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma s^2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma cs\).
  2. By (3.51), the strains of the rectangle are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma c^2/E_{\mathrm{x}} - \nu_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\sigma s^2/E_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\sigma c^2/E_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma s^2/E_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma cs/G_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  3. We substitute into \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,c^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,s^2 + \gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\,cs\) from step 3, which measures the elongation of the diagonal, and multiply out:
    \[\frac{\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\sigma} = \frac{c^4}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} - c^2 s^2\,\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} - c^2 s^2\,\frac{\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} + \frac{s^4}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} + \frac{c^2 s^2}{G_{\mathrm{xy}}} .\]
  4. By the reciprocal relation (3.43), \(\nu_{\mathrm{yx}}/E_{\mathrm{y}} = \nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\), so the two middle terms combine into \(-2c^2 s^2\,\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  5. The modulus \(\bar E = \sigma/\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the reciprocal of this expression:
    \[\frac{1}{\bar E} = \frac{c^4}{E_{\mathrm{x}}} + \frac{s^4}{E_{\mathrm{y}}} + c^2 s^2 \left(\frac{1}{G_{\mathrm{xy}}} - \frac{2\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}}{E_{\mathrm{x}}}\right) . \tag{3.52}\]

For \(c = 1\), \(s = 0\) the equation gives \(\bar E = E_{\mathrm{x}}\), and for \(c = 0\), \(s = 1\) it gives \(\bar E = E_{\mathrm{y}}\), as it must. The three terms are the three parts of the displacement in figure 3.152: the first is the stretch along the fibres, the second the stretch across them, and the third the sliding of the layers, reduced by the lateral contraction of the two tensions. The derivation uses only Cauchy's formula for the bar, the compliance relation of the plate and the rule for the strain of a fibre. CM computes the strains of a vessel wound from fibres along the same route, with \(\sin\theta = 0{,}8\) and \(\cos\theta = 0{,}6\) (CM Example 6.3.1, PDF pp. 268-269). The sources do not give equation (3.52) in the form we write here. The table gives the modulus for a few directions in which \(c\) and \(s\) are fractions:

\(c\) \(s\) \(\bar E\) (GPa)
\(1\) \(0\) \(205{,}0\)
\(40/41 = 0{,}9756\) \(9/41 = 0{,}2195\) \(82{,}11\)
\(24/25 = 0{,}96\) \(7/25 = 0{,}28\) \(60{,}18\)
\(12/13 = 0{,}9231\) \(5/13 = 0{,}3846\) \(37{,}85\)
\(4/5 = 0{,}8\) \(3/5 = 0{,}6\) \(18{,}95\)
\(3/5 = 0{,}6\) \(4/5 = 0{,}8\) \(12{,}59\)
\(0\) \(1\) \(10{,}00\)

Already at a small deviation from the fibres, \(s = 0{,}2195\), the modulus drops from \(205\) GPa to \(82{,}11\) GPa, to \(40\) percent. Why so fast? Let us look at the terms of (3.52) for \(c = 40/41\) and \(s = 9/41\). The first term is \(c^4/E_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}004419\) GPa\(^{-1}\), the second \(s^4/E_{\mathrm{y}} = 0{,}000232\) GPa\(^{-1}\), and the third \(c^2 s^2\,(1/G_{\mathrm{xy}} - 2\nu_{\mathrm{xy}}/E_{\mathrm{x}}) = 0{,}007528\) GPa\(^{-1}\), already larger than the first. The number in the bracket of the third term is \(1/6 - 2 \cdot 0{,}26/205 = 0{,}1641\) GPa\(^{-1}\), which is about \(34\) times more than \(1/E_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}004878\) GPa\(^{-1}\), because the shear modulus \(G_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is so small. The small factor \(c^2 s^2 = 0{,}0459\) does not make up for this. A slightly inclined strip therefore does not stretch through the stiff fibres but through the sliding of the layers between them. Figure 3.155 shows the modulus in all directions in the plane of the plate.

On the left is the blue curve: in each direction its distance from the centre is proportional to the modulus, \(205\) GPa in the direction of the fibres. The directions are measured from the grey lines of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The grey dashed circle is steel, which has \(196\) GPa in every direction. The small frame around the centre is enlarged six times on the right in the large frame, where the curve and its axes are drawn. The first dot is the direction with \(c = 0{,}8\) (\(18{,}95\) GPa), the second the direction with \(c = 0{,}6\) (\(12{,}59\) GPa). The dot in the left part of the figure is the direction with \(c = 40/41\) (\(82{,}11\) GPa), barely inclined from the fibres, and the modulus is already below one half. The axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) are at the lower right.

Wood is similar to the composite, except that its material axes are not straight. The fibres run along the trunk, and the growth rings, layers the tree adds every year, are rings around the pith (figure 3.106, left). The direction along the fibres, the direction outward from the pith and the direction along the growth ring therefore change from point to point (SADD, PDF p. 331). A small piece cut far from the pith, where the growth rings are nearly straight, we treat as orthotropic with the material axes in these three directions. SADD gives wood as an example of an orthotropic material (SADD, PDF p. 335). Young's modulus along the fibres of wood is \(9\) to \(16\) GPa (BOWER Table 3.1, PDF p. 100).

Let us also say how we arrived at these results. From the 81 numbers of the generalized Hooke's law the symmetry of stress and strain led us to 36 (lemma 3.26 on swapping the indices within a pair), and the assumption of a symmetric material stiffness matrix to 21. Then for each plane of material symmetry we compared the law in two systems that differ in the direction of one axis, like a cube and its mirror image across the plane. The components with one index of this axis changed sign, the constants did not, and this set to zero every constant that relates such a component to a component that does not change sign (lemma 3.31 on zeros due to a plane of material symmetry). One plane gave 13 constants, three perpendicular ones 9. The turns about an axis by a quarter revolution and onto the diagonals gave 5, and five constants are enough for the material to be the same under every turn about this axis. The same turns about two axes gave 2, exactly Hooke's law of an isotropic material. What remained open is the promise that the material stiffness matrix is symmetric, which we used in counting and in the reciprocal relations. We will show it with the work that the stresses do when the material deforms. The force that slowly stretches a bar or a strip changes during the stretching, and for the work of such a force we need a new mathematical tool that adds up very many very small contributions. We continue with it in the next section.
